rationale:
structural: The only structural obligation in the text is the prescribed signature: `impl Sources { pub async fn list(&self, scope: &SourceScope) -> Result<Vec<PathBuf>, SourceError>; }`. An alternative such as a free function, a different receiver, or a different return type (for example `Vec<ResourceId>`) would produce the same listing but violate that clause, so the obligation is real.

`crates/trust-but-verify/src/sources/public.rs#impl[Sources]/fn[list]` declares exactly that signature. It is `pub async`, takes `&self` and `&SourceScope`, and returns `Result<Vec<PathBuf>, SourceError>`. It delegates to the provider and maps each `ResourceId` to `PathBuf::from(id.location)`. This root meets the whole obligation.

`crates/trust-but-verify/src/sources.rs#trait[SourceProvider]/fn[list]` is a different signature. It returns `Vec<ResourceId>` with `Self::Error`, and `Sources::list` reaches it by delegation. The requirement does not prescribe it, so it needs no reference. Its marker is harmless, and no further root is missing.

behavioral: `requirements.sdk.graph.validation-context.list_sources.fn` only declares the Rust signature `Sources::list(&self, scope: &SourceScope) -> Result<Vec<PathBuf>, SourceError>`. It has no MUST, MUST NOT or SHOULD clause. The doc comment "List file identities within this scope" restates the behavior that the separate `requirements.sdk.graph.validation-context.list_sources.behavior` requirement governs. So this requirement states a structural obligation: the type and method shape, which the compiler enforces. It has no independent observable behavioral obligation that needs test evidence here. It has no `Tests` edges, and none are needed. The requirement has `Implements` edges for the signature, and I did not reassess them. Any behavioral checking of listing belongs to `list_sources.behavior`, which this assessment does not cover.
